newsitem.title: INDIA: March sales to boost India TELCO's net.
newsitem.headline: March sales to boost India TELCO's net.

text.p: India's leading truckmaker Tata Engineering & Locomotive Company (TELCO) will see net profit surge some 35 percent in the year ended March 31, 1997, despite an overall industrial slowdown, analysts said on Monday.
TELCO's shares closed 8.50 rupees, or two percent, higher at 400 on the Bombay Stock Exchange on Monday as speculators bought ahead of the earnings announcement due on Tuesday.
Analysts polled ahead of TELCO's 1996/97 results forecast an average net profit of 7.20 billion rupees, up 36 percent from 5.3 billion in the previous year.
Lower demand for vehicles forced most automobile firms to slash production during the year and TELCO cut its output from a target of around 240,000 units to 218,393 units in 1996/97.
"There was definitely a slowdown in sales too," said Anupam Thareja, automobile analyst at HSBC B&K Securities. Sales growth slowed to 18.6 percent from 31 percent in 1995/96.
"But March was phenomenally good," Thareja said.
Most analysts raised their net forecasts for TELCO after sharply improved March sales figures were released last month.
"March sales were higher than expected," said K.N. Sreenivasan, automobile analyst at securities firm Jardine Fleming India Broking.
TELCO sold 29,190 units in March, up from 22,283 vehicles in the same month of 1996. The company sold an average 16,900 vehicles in the first eleven months of 1996/97.
Analysts had pegged March sales at around 22,000 units as vehicle sales generally pick up during the last month of the fiscal year when buyers take advantage of depreciation benefits.
A Reuters poll of leading analysts, released before the March automobile figures were out, had forecast an average net profit of 6.82 billion rupees.
"I was looking at total sales of around 206,000 units but the company has sold 215,276 units during the year," Sreenivasan said. TELCO sold 181,383 vehicles in 1995/96.
Analysts said inventories with dealers had risen and the higher inventories would hit first quarter 1997/98 sales.
Unofficial April automobile data -- due to be released next week -- show that TELCO's April sales have fallen to 10,051 units from 14,203 units in April 1996.
"They seem to have pushed vehicle sales onto their dealers at the end of the year and they might have to slow down production in the first half of 1997/98," said an analyst at a foreign broking firm.
Jardine's Sreenivasan recommended a medium- to long-term buy on the stock.
"On a three-month view the stock will underperform depending on the magnitude of the expected hike in diesel prices but fundamentally it's a very solid company," he said.
